newsitem.title: USA: Archer seeks to pare down ethanol subsidy.
newsitem.headline: Archer seeks to pare down ethanol subsidy.

text.p: House tax writer Bill Archer Monday said he wants to pare down the subsidy for ethanol, the alternative motor fuel made from corn, and farm state lawmakers and agriculture groups vowed to fight the move.
In his tax package unveiled Monday, the chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee proposed shaving the 5.4 cent-per-gallon tax credit by 0.3 cent and doing away with it in the year 2000.

The Texas Republican also proposed a penalty on "excess" ethanol production, an increase in tax credits allowed for small ethanol producers and, within limits, the immediate repeal of subsidies for ETBE, a competitor fuel.

Overall, the proposals on ethanol would bring the government an additional $4.1 billion over the next decade, money that will be used to help offset billions of dollars in tax cuts called for in the tax package.
Archer told a news conference the ethanol tax break diverted corn to an artificial, industrial use at the same time the world needed more food.
"If there were ever an anachronistic provision in the tax code, it is this one," he said. "It makes absolutely no sense. It should be removed."
Farm-state lawmakers and ethanol backers said they were vehemently opposed to any tinkering with the tax break, which experts say is worth billions of dollars a year to farmers.
"The bottom line is it's in place and it shouldn't be tampered with," said Ron McCartney, an Iowa soybean and corn farmer and member of the National Corn Growers Association.
"Our group is unalterably opposed to this," said Eric Vaughn, president of the Renewable Fuels Association.
"It almost seems vindictive," he added, because the plan reduces the fuel tax break without raising very much revenue for the government.

Rep. Jim Nussle, an Iowa Republican who sits on the Ways and Means Comittee, said he would file an amendment Wednesday to strip any ethanol language from the tax bill. "Any modification of the current ethanol tax credit is unacceptable," he said.
Nussle said it was not clear yet whether ethanol backers had the votes in the committee to beat Archer. He also said he did not expect any help from the House leadership, unlike in years past.
"The discussions with the leadership have been positive,but we understand that at a least for the time being we're on our own and we will do battle accordingly," he said.
Archer has been gunning for the tax break for years. In 1995, the provision narrowly escaped the chairman's budget chopping block when House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia stepped in.

The ethanol subsidy was born of the 1970s oil crisis when the government wanted to provide incentives to producers of alternative fuels. In 1990, Congress passed a law guaranteeing the tax credit until the year 2000.
Agriculture analyst John Urbanchuk, of AUS Consultants, said that by going slow on ethanol now, Archer was aiming at ending the tax break by 2000.
"Probably, politically it is setting the stage for elimination in the year 2000," Urbanchuck said.
